beur-hagra/1:א: (א) Seif 1, 'anything.' In accordance with Rabbi Yochanan there, who adds to [the ruling of] Shmuel — for [Shmuel] had only prohibited types of meat, and ardilaya is a type of fowl. Ran.
beur-hagra/1:ב: (ב) 'And he should not eat it.' In accordance with Rav, as Shmuel and Rabbi Yochanan add to [the ruling of] Rav, and as the Ran wrote.
beur-hagra/1:ג: (ג) 'That it is no better.' Meaning not like Tosafot there who wrote that Rava's case does not apply to matzah in our time, and the baraita that it exists is in Pesach specifically; and the incident of Rava in Taanit who learned from Pesach — but for us who hold all this applies also to matzah, as stated in seif 2; and all this is because of stringency lest they uproot — see Rashbam there, all the more here where it also applies to matzah.
beur-hagra/2:א: (א) Seif 2 — one who sleeps, etc. Rashbam explains it refers to the beginning because we hold the incident of Rava; but Rambam explains Rava was alone, and therefore 'one who sleeps.' And this requires further study, for Abaye was raised there in his house, as stated: when we were at Rava's house we would sing, etc.
beur-hagra/2:ב: (ב) 'Members of a group,' etc. Mishna there; see BeHag.
beur-hagra/2:ג: (ג) 'And all this only applies,' etc. Rashbam in the Mishna, and as written 'if one may conclude,' etc. — that they should not uproot, etc., as above.
chok-yaakov/1:א: (א) One may not eat. And after the fact if he ate he need not return and eat afikoman; see above siman 477 seif 105. And from the Mechaber's writing "one may not eat" it is implied that to drink is fine, as Tur wrote in siman 481 — like one who drinks the other two cups; only after the cups it is forbidden to drink intoxicating beverages specifically, as all this is explained explicitly below in siman 481, see there; and so is implied in Taz siman 479 seif 2. And such is the essential ruling — not as Magen Avraham wrote plainly that just as it is forbidden to eat, so it is forbidden to drink; that is the view of Rif brought in Tur siman 481, and that is not the agreement of the poskim.
chok-yaakov/1:ב: (ב) In two places. And Magen Avraham wrote: even in one house at two tables.
chok-yaakov/2:א: (א) That some of them slept — in Tur and Rokeach siman 488 and in Rashbam's explanation and Ra'avad and Rosh and Agudah chapter Afikoman it is explained: whenever some fell into deep sleep they may not eat, unless when some merely dozed; and they explained thus — R' Yehuda's words refer to the beginning, and so is the simple meaning of the Gemara there; but Rambam and Ra'avad explained R' Yehuda refers to the end — if some slept they may eat; and the Mechaber ruled like them; see Levush who ruled like the first view, which is Rosh and his supporters; and so appears to be the essence.
chok-yaakov/2:ב: (ב) But sleep before that — even during the meal it is of no consequence, not like Maharil, so wrote in Darkei Moshe.
peri-megadim/1:_: After afikoman. Taz: afikoman means a commemoration of Pesach, and it is forbidden to eat in two places like Pesach which is forbidden; and also one may not eat even in one place other things after afikoman, like Pesach. And for Rashi and Rashbam, afikoman is matza of mitzvah, and at first they bless on it — Magen Avraham — because after one filled his stomach one does not bless; per them one does not eat other things after afikoman, but in two places one could say it is permitted per Rashi and Rashbam; see Pesachim 120a and siman 477, and see in Magen Avraham 3 I will explain that even per Rashi and Rashbam one may not eat afikoman in two places. And all poskim ruled there — even though it is d'rabbanan, the anonymous ruling is like them, and the dispute is per Mar Zutra; see Rif and Rosh Pesachim 120a, and see in 482 it will be explained further, see there. See Levush: since afikoman is in place of Pesach, one may not eat after it — it is somewhat difficult, for even per Rashi and Rashbam that it is obligatory matza, one may not eat after it. He further wrote: afikoman — afiku mani, meaning they brought out all types of sweetness (from the word man and the like); and 'ein maftirin' — they do not open their mouths (like 'yafteru befisa' — pours water) to say afikoman after Pesach and after matza, etc. Some explain 'ein maftirin' like one who takes leave of his friend and goes from him — and the explanation: they do not take leave and go from Pesach to say afikoman. Another explanation: for matza itself they call afikoman, since it is dear to us and sweet like man and types of sweetness, see there. And behold the explanation afiku mani is also true — that one does not eat in two places, and to say afiku kelim — take utensils from here and go to another place; see Pesachim 119b.
